finding.claim: /transfer accepts negative amounts, so a sender can pull funds out of any recipient's account and credit their own.
finding.source: bank.py:10 request.json["amount"], a client-supplied JSON value with no sign or type check.
finding.sink: bank.py:13-14 BAL[g.user] -= amount and BAL[to] += amount, which move balances between accounts.

trace.note: amount is read from the request body unvalidated
the only guard is BAL[g.user] < amount; with amount = -50 and balance 0, 0 < -50 is False so the check passes

finding.guards_checked: Line 11 checks sufficiency only, not sign. /withdraw rejects amount <= 0 at line 21, so the same check is missing from /transfer. No other validation exists in the file. Any account name present in BAL can be targeted via 'to'.

verdict.guard_found: None in bank.py that blocks negative amounts on /transfer. Line 11 checks only sufficiency (BAL[g.user] < amount), and a negative amount passes it. /withdraw's sign check at line 21 is not applied to /transfer. g.user is set outside this file, so any authentication there is not visible, but it only limits who the attacker is.
verdict.reason: bank.py:10 takes amount unvalidated and bank.py:11 only checks BAL[g.user] < amount, so amount=-50 passes and bank.py:13-14 move funds from the recipient to the sender; the attacker only needs to be a valid account holder, which is a low-privilege role.

finding.claim: NaN or -Infinity amounts bypass the balance check and corrupt balances, which lets an attacker make a balance unbounded and then transfer or withdraw arbitrary sums.
finding.source: bank.py:10 and bank.py:20, where request.json parses the 'amount' field. Python's json module accepts the non-standard literals NaN and -Infinity by default, so they reach the code as floats.
finding.sink: bank.py:13 and bank.py:14 in /transfer, and bank.py:23 in /withdraw, where balances are mutated.

trace.note: amount = NaN or -inf from the JSON body
BAL < NaN is always False, and BAL < -inf is False, so the check passes
BAL[me] -= amount sets the attacker's balance to NaN or +inf
BAL[to] += amount sets the recipient's balance to NaN or -inf
on later calls, NaN < x and inf < x are False for any finite x, so every subsequent transfer passes the check regardless of size
/withdraw has the same issue: NaN passes both checks (NaN <= 0 is False, BAL < NaN is False). -inf is stopped by amount <= 0, but NaN is not
BAL[me] -= amount then keeps the balance at NaN or inf, so the attacker can withdraw without limit

finding.guards_checked: Line 11 uses < comparisons, which return False for NaN and do not catch -inf. Line 21 catches only amount <= 0, which does not stop NaN. There is no math.isfinite, no isinstance(float/int) check, and no bounds check anywhere in the file. Not run: the parser behaviour is from the Python and Flask documentation and was not executed here.

verdict.guard_found: none. bank.py:11 is a plain `<` check that is False for NaN and for -inf, so it passes. bank.py:21 only rejects `amount <= 0`, which is False for NaN. No isfinite, isinstance, or bounds check exists in bank.py.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: bank.py:10 and :20 read the JSON amount, bank.py:11 and :21 compare with `<` or `<=` and so pass NaN and -inf, and bank.py:13-14 and :23 mutate balances. Any caller that can reach /transfer or /withdraw can trigger this, since g.user is set outside this file and no validation exists here. The only assumption not checked in this directory is that Flask's request.json uses Python's json.loads, which accepts NaN and Infinity by default.

finding.claim: The balance check and the debit are not atomic, so concurrent requests can overdraw an account (double spend).
finding.source: Any client that can send concurrent POSTs to /transfer or /withdraw, with amount chosen by the client (bank.py:10, bank.py:20).
finding.sink: bank.py:13 and bank.py:23, where the balance is debited after a separate check.

trace.note: no lock is held between the check and the debit
debit BAL[g.user]; a second thread that also passed line 11 has already been scheduled, so both debits apply and the balance goes negative

finding.guards_checked: No lock, transaction, or atomic operation exists in the file. The BAL dict is shared module-level state. Exploitability depends on the deployment: a threaded or multi-process WSGI server would expose this, but the server configuration is not in the repository. Confidence is medium.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are the balance comparisons at bank.py:11 and bank.py:21, which run before the debit with no lock, transaction, or atomic update between them, so they do not prevent a race. Nothing in the repo sets g.user, so no authentication guard is visible either.
verdict.reason: The check-then-debit at bank.py:11-13 and bank.py:21-23 is a real non-atomic pattern on shared BAL, but exploitability depends on the server running request handlers concurrently, which is not in the repo (no app.run or WSGI config), and g.user is read at bank.py:11, 13, 21, 23 without being set anywhere in the repo, so the attacker's role and reachability cannot be confirmed from the code available.

finding.claim: An unknown or unhashable 'to' raises after the sender has already been debited, so the funds are lost and the transfer is not rolled back.
finding.source: bank.py:9 request.json["to"], a client-supplied value that is not validated.
finding.sink: bank.py:13, the sender debit, which executes before the recipient credit at bank.py:14.

trace.note: to is read from the body without checking that it names an existing account
BAL[g.user] -= amount has already been committed to the in-memory dict
BAL[to] raises KeyError (or TypeError for a list or dict key); the request returns 500 and nothing reverts the debit

finding.guards_checked: There is no existence check on 'to' and no try/except or rollback. The sender only loses their own funds, so this is an integrity and atomicity defect rather than a theft path.

verdict.guard_found: none. bank.py:9 reads `to` with no existence check, bank.py:11 checks only the sender's balance, and bank.py:13 debits BAL[g.user] before bank.py:14 reads BAL[to]. Nothing in the file wraps this in try/except or rolls back the debit.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: bank.py:13 commits the debit to the in-memory BAL dict, then bank.py:14 raises KeyError (or TypeError for an unhashable key) when `to` is unknown, and no rollback exists, so the sender loses funds. The attacker only needs whatever access reaches /transfer, which is at least a user whose g.user is set (set outside this file), and the only party harmed is the sender, so this is an atomicity defect with no theft path rather than a security vulnerability.
